danish.title: Tiende bog (1812) — Kapitel 14
paragraphs: »Nå, er hun køn? Åh, ven — min lyserøde er uimodståelig; hun hedder Dunjasja....«
Men da han så Rostovs ansigt, holdt Iljin inde. Han så, at hans helt og fører fulgte en helt anden tankegang.
Rostov sendte Iljin et vredt blik og gik uden at svare med hurtige skridt mod landsbyen.
»Jeg skal vise dem; jeg skal give dem, de røvere!« sagde han for sig selv.
Alpatytj fulgte ham i en glidende trav og havde nær ikke kunnet holde trit.
»Hvilken beslutning har De behaget at træffe?« sagde han.
Rostov standsede og vendte sig pludselig og strengt mod Alpatytj med knyttede næver.

»Beslutning? Hvilken beslutning? Gamle tåbe!...« råbte han. »Hvad har du stillet op? Hva'? Bønderne gør oprør, og du kan ikke styre dem? Du er selv en forræder! Jeg flår jer alle levende!...« Og som om han var bange for at spilde sit forråd af vrede, forlod han Alpatytj og gik hurtigt videre. Alpatytj beherskede sine krænkede følelser og holdt trit med Rostov i sin glidende gang, mens han fortsatte med at fremlægge sine synspunkter. Han sagde, at bønderne var genstridige, og at det i øjeblikket ville være uklogt at »overkomme« dem uden en bevæbnet styrke, og om det ikke ville være bedre først at sende bud efter militæret?
»Jeg skal give dem bevæbnet styrke... Jeg skal 'overkomme' dem!« udstødte Rostov meningsløst, åndeløs af vanvittig, dyrisk raseri og trangen til at give den afløb.

Uden at tænke over, hvad han ville gøre, bevægede han sig ubevidst med hurtige, beslutsomme skridt mod mængden. Og jo nærmere han kom, jo mere følte Alpatytj, at denne uberegnelige handling måske kunne give gode resultater. Bønderne i mængden blev på samme måde slået, da de så Rostovs hurtige, faste skridt og beslutsomme, mørke ansigt.

Efter at husarerne var kommet til landsbyen, og Rostov var gået for at se fyrstinden, var der opstået en vis forvirring og uenighed i mængden. Nogle af bønderne sagde, at disse nyankomne var russere og kunne tage det ilde op, at fruen blev tilbageholdt. Dron var af denne mening, men så snart han udtrykte den, angreb Karp og andre deres forhenværende ældste.

»Hvor mange år har du ikke mæsket dig på kommunen?« råbte Karp ad ham. »Det er dig ligegyldigt! Du graver din pengekrukke op og tager den med dig.... Hvad rager det dig, om vores hjem bliver ødelagt eller ej?«
»Vi har fået besked på at holde orden, og at ingen må forlade hjemmene eller tage et eneste korn med, og det er det hele!« råbte en anden.

»Det var din søns tur til at blive udskrevet, men nej! Du var for nærig til at undvære din klods af en søn,« begyndte en lille gammel mand pludselig at angribe Dron — »og så tog de min Vanka til soldat i stedet! Men vi skal alle dø.«
»Det er sikkert, vi skal alle dø. Jeg har ikke noget imod kommunen,« sagde Dron.
»Det er nemt at sige — ikke noget imod den! Du har fyldt maven....«

De to høje bønder sagde deres mening. Så snart Rostov, fulgt af Iljin, Lavrusjka og Alpatytj, nærmede sig mængden, trådte Karp frem med fingrene stukket i bæltet og et lille smil. Dron trak sig derimod tilbage, og mængden rykkede tættere sammen.
»Hvem er jeres ældste her? Hej?« råbte Rostov, idet han nærmede sig mængden med hurtige skridt.
»Den ældste? Hvad vil De med ham?...« spurgte Karp.
Men før ordene rigtig var ude af munden på ham, fløj hans kasket af, og et voldsomt slag slog hans hoved til siden.
»Huerne af, forrædere!« råbte Rostov med en vredens stemme. »Hvor er den ældste?« skreg han rasende.
»Den ældste.... Han vil have den ældste!... Dron Zakharytj, det er dig!« lød spagfærdige og forfippede stemmer her og der, og huerne begyndte at komme af.
»Vi gør ikke oprør, vi følger ordrerne,« erklærede Karp, og i samme øjeblik begyndte flere stemmer at tale på én gang.
»Det er, som de gamle har bestemt — der er for mange af jer, der kommanderer.«

»Diskutere? Mytteri!... Røvere! Forrædere!« råbte Rostov meningsløst med en stemme, der ikke var hans egen, mens han greb Karp i kraven. »Bind ham, bind ham!« skreg han, selvom der ikke var nogen til at binde ham ud over Lavrusjka og Alpatytj.
Lavrusjka løb dog hen til Karp og greb ham i armene bagfra.
»Skal jeg kalde på vores folk hinsides bakken?« råbte han.
Alpatytj vendte sig mod bønderne og befalede to af dem ved navn at komme og binde Karp. Mændene trådte lydigt ud af mængden og begyndte at tage bælterne af.
»Hvor er den ældste?« forlangte Rostov med høj stemme.
Med et blegt og sammenbidt ansigt trådte Dron ud af mængden.
»Er det dig, der er ældste? Bind ham, Lavrusjka!« råbte Rostov, som om heller ikke den befaling kunne møde modstand.
Og faktisk begyndte to bønder mere at binde Dron, der selv tog sit bælte af og rakte det til dem, som for at hjælpe dem.
»Og I hører alle efter!« sagde Rostov til bønderne. »Gå straks hjem, og lad mig ikke høre en eneste lyd fra jer!«
»Åh, vi har jo ikke gjort noget galt! Vi handlede bare af dumhed. Det er det rene vrøvl.... Jeg sagde dengang, at det ikke var i orden,« lød bikkende stemmer.
»Der kan I se! Hvad sagde jeg?« sagde Alpatytj og kom til sig selv igen. »Det er forkert, drenge!«
»Det var bare vores dumhed, Jakov Alpatytj,« lød svarene, og mængden begyndte straks at spredes gennem landsbyen.
De to bundne mænd blev ført til herregården. De to berusede bønder fulgte efter dem.
»Nå, når jeg ser på dig!...« sagde den ene til Karp.
»Hvordan kan man tale sådan til herskaberne? Hvad tænkte du på, din tosse?« tilføjede den anden — »Sikke en fjols!«

To timer senere stod vognene i gården til huset i Bogutjarovo. Bønderne bar travlt ejendommene ud og pakkede dem på vognene, og Dron, der på fyrstinde Marjas ønske var blevet befriet fra det skab, han havde været lukket inde i, stod i gården og dirigerede mændene.

»Pas nu på med det der,« sagde en af bønderne, en mand med et rundt, smilende ansigt, der tog en kiste fra en stuepige. »Det har jo kostet penge! Hvordan kan du bare smide det derind eller proppe det under snoren, hvor det bliver slidt? Jeg bryder mig ikke om den måde at gøre tingene på. Lad det hele blive gjort ordentligt, som sig hør og bør. Se her, læg det under bastmåtten og dæk det med hø — så er det!«
»Åh! Bøger, bøger!« sagde en anden bonde, der bar fyrst Andrejs bogskabe ud. »Pas på, du ikke støder dem! Tungt er det, drenge — lutter bøger.«
»Ja, de arbejdede hele dagen og legede ikke!« bemærkede den høje, rundhovedet bonde alvorligt og pegede med et betegnende blink på ordbøgerne øverst.

Da Rostov ikke ønskede at trænge sig på hos fyrstinden, gik han ikke tilbage til huset, men blev i landsbyen og ventede på hendes afrejse. Da hendes vogn kørte ud fra huset, steg han til hest og ledsagede hende halvanden mil fra Bogutjarovo til det sted, hvor vejen var besat af russiske tropper. Ved kroen i Jankovo tog han ærbødigt afsked med hende og tillod sig for første gang at kysse hendes hånd.

»Hvad siger De dog!« svarede han rødmende til fyrstinde Marjas takkende ord for hendes befrielse, som hun kaldte det, der var sket. »Enhver politibetjent ville have gjort det samme! Hvis vi kun havde haft bønder at kæmpe mod, ville vi ikke have ladet fjenden nå så langt,« sagde han med en følelse af skam og et ønske om at skifte emne. »Jeg er kun glad for at have haft lejlighed til at stifte bekendtskab med Dem. Farvel, fyrstinde. Jeg ønsker Dem lykke og trøst og håber at møde Dem igen under lykkeligere omstændigheder. Hvis De ikke vil få mig til at rødme, beder jeg Dem lade være med at takke mig!«

Men fyrstinden, om hun end ikke takkede ham igen med ord, takkede ham med hele sit ansigts udtryk, strålende af taknemmelighed og ømhed. Hun kunne ikke tro, at der ikke var noget at takke ham for. Tværtimod syntes det hende sikkert, at uden ham ville hun være omkommet i hænderne på oprørerne og franskmændene, og at han havde udsat sig for forfærdelig og åbenbar fare for at redde hende, og endnu mere sikkert var det, at han var en mand med en ædel og ophøjet sjæl, der var i stand til at forstå hendes situation og hendes sorg. Hans venlige, ærlige øjne, med tårerne, der steg op i dem, da hun selv begyndte at græde, mens hun fortalte om sit tab, forlod ikke hendes erindring.
Da hun havde taget afsked med ham og var alene, følte hun pludselig sine øjne fyldes med tårer, og da trængte det mærkelige spørgsmål sig på for første gang: elskede hun ham?

Resten af vejen til Moskva, selvom fyrstindens situation ikke var munter, lagde Dunjasja, der kørte med hende i vognen, mere end én gang mærke til, at hendes frue lænede sig ud af vinduet og smilede med et udtryk af blandet glæde og sorg.
»Nå, og hvis jeg nu elsker ham?« tænkte fyrstinde Marja.

Selvom hun skammede sig over at indrømme for sig selv, at hun var faldet for en mand, der måske aldrig ville elske hende, trøstede hun sig med tanken om, at ingen nogensinde ville få det at vide, og at hun ikke ville være at bebrejde, hvis hun uden nogensinde at tale om det til nogen fortsatte til sit livs ende med at elske den mand, som hun var faldet for, for første og sidste gang i sit liv.

Undertiden, når hun genkaldte sig hans blik, hans medfølelse og hans ord, forekom lykken hende ikke umulig. Det var i de øjeblikke, at Dunjasja lagde mærke til hendes smil, når hun kiggede ud af vognen.

»Var det ikke skæbnen, der førte ham til Bogutjarovo, og netop i det øjeblik?« tænkte fyrstinde Marja. »Og som fik hans søster til at afslå min bror?« Og i alt dette så fyrstinde Marja forsynets hånd.

Det indtryk, fyrstinden gjorde på Rostov, var meget behageligt. At mindes hende gav ham glæde, og når hans kammerater, der hørte om hans eventyr i Bogutjarovo, drillede ham med, at han var redet ud efter hø og i stedet havde snuppet en af Ruslands rigeste arvinger, blev han vred. Det gjorde ham vred netop fordi tanken om at gifte sig med den bløde fyrstinde Marja, der tiltrak ham og besad en uhyre formue, mod hans vilje mere end én gang var trængt ind i hans hoved. For sig selv kunne Nikolaj ikke ønske sig en bedre hustru: ved at gifte sig med hende ville han gøre sin mor, grevinden, lykkelig, kunne bringe orden i sin fars affærer og endda — det følte han — sikre fyrstinde Marjas lykke.
Men Sonja? Og hans troskabsløfte? Det var grunden til, at Rostov blev vred, når man drillede ham med fyrstinde Bolkonskaja.

english.title: Book Ten (1812) — Chapter 14
paragraphs: "So, is she pretty? Oh, friend—my pink one is delicious; her name's Dunyasha..."
But glancing at Rostov's face, Ilyin stopped short. He could see that his hero and commander was following an entirely different train of thought.
Rostov glanced angrily at Ilyin and without replying strode rapidly toward the village.
"I'll show them; I'll give it to them, the scoundrels!" he said to himself.
Alpatych, at a gliding trot, just barely managing not to run, kept up with him with difficulty.
"What decision have you been pleased to reach?" he said.
Rostov stopped and, clenching his fists, suddenly turned on Alpatych with fierce intensity.

"Decision? What decision? Old fool!" he cried. "What have you been doing? The peasants are rioting and you can't control them? You're a traitor yourself! I know you. I'll skin you all alive!" And as if afraid of wasting his store of anger, he left Alpatych and strode rapidly forward. Alpatych, mastering his offended feelings, kept pace with Rostov at a gliding gait and continued to share his views. He said the peasants were obstinate and that at this moment it would be unwise to confront them without armed force—wouldn't it be better to send for the military first?
"I'll give them armed force... I'll confront them!" Rostov uttered meaninglessly, breathless with irrational animal fury and the need to vent it.

Without thinking about what he would do, he moved unconsciously with quick, resolute steps toward the crowd. And the closer he got, the more Alpatych felt that this reckless action might actually produce good results. The peasants in the crowd were similarly affected when they saw Rostov's rapid, firm steps and resolute, frowning face.

After the hussars had come to the village and Rostov had gone to see the princess, a certain confusion and division had arisen among the crowd. Some peasants said these newcomers were Russians and might take offense that the mistress was being detained. Dron shared this opinion, but as soon as he expressed it, Karp and others attacked their former Elder.

"How many years have you been fattening off the commune?" Karp shouted at him. "It's all the same to you! You'll dig up your buried pot of money and take it with you... What do you care whether our homes are destroyed or not?"
"We were told to keep order, that nobody's to leave their homes or take a single grain—and that's that!" cried another.

"It was your son's turn to be drafted, but oh no! You were too stingy to part with your big lump of a boy," a little old man suddenly began attacking Dron—"so they took my Vanka and shaved him for a soldier! But we all have to die."
"Sure, we all have to die. I'm not against the commune," said Dron.
"That's right—not against it! You've stuffed your belly..."

The two tall peasants had their say. As soon as Rostov, followed by Ilyin, Lavrushka, and Alpatych, came up to the crowd, Karp, thrusting his fingers into his belt and smiling slightly, moved to the front. Dron, on the contrary, slipped to the rear, and the crowd drew closer together.
"Who's your Elder here? Hey!" shouted Rostov, coming up to the crowd with quick steps.
"The Elder? What do you want with him?" asked Karp.
But before the words were fully out of his mouth, his cap flew off and a fierce blow jerked his head to one side.
"Caps off, traitors!" shouted Rostov furiously. "Where's the Elder?" he demanded.
"The Elder... He wants the Elder!... Dron Zakharych, you!" meek and flustered voices were heard here and there, and caps began to come off.
"We're not rioting, we're following orders," declared Karp, and at that moment several voices began speaking at once.
"It's as the old men decided—there's too many of you giving orders."

"Arguing? Mutiny!... Traitors!" cried Rostov meaninglessly in a voice not his own, gripping Karp by the collar. "Tie him up! Tie him up!" he shouted, though there was no one to do it except Lavrushka and Alpatych.
Lavrushka, however, ran up to Karp and seized his arms from behind.
"Shall I call our men from beyond the hill?" he called out.
Alpatych turned to the peasants and ordered two of them by name to come and bind Karp. The men obediently stepped out of the crowd and began taking off their belts.
"Where's the Elder?" demanded Rostov in a loud voice.
With a pale and frowning face, Dron stepped out of the crowd.
"Are you the Elder? Bind him, Lavrushka!" shouted Rostov, as if that command too could not possibly meet with any resistance.
And in fact two more peasants began tying Dron, who took off his own belt and handed it to them, as if to help.
"And all of you—listen to me!" said Rostov to the peasants. "Get back to your homes at once, and don't let me hear another word out of you!"
"Why, we haven't done anything wrong! We were just being foolish. It's all nonsense... I said at the time it wasn't proper," voices were heard grumbling.
"There! What did I tell you?" said Alpatych, coming into his own again. "It's wrong, boys!"
"All our foolishness, Yakov Alpatych," came the answers, and the crowd immediately began to disperse through the village.
The two bound men were led off to the manor house. The two drunken peasants followed them.
"Aye, look at you!" said one of them to Karp.
"How can you talk to the masters like that? What were you thinking, you fool?" added the other. "A real fool!"

Two hours later the carts stood in the courtyard of the Bogucharovo house. The peasants were briskly carrying out the proprietor's belongings and loading them onto the carts, and Dron, freed at Princess Mary's request from the room where he had been locked up, stood in the yard directing the men.

"Don't just throw it in like that," said one peasant, a man with a round, smiling face, taking a casket from a housemaid. "That cost good money! You can't just chuck it in or shove it under the rope where it'll get scratched. I don't like sloppy work. Let it all be done properly, by the book. Look—put it under the bast matting and cover it with hay—that's the way!"
"Books, books!" said another peasant, carrying out Prince Andrew's bookcases. "Careful—don't bump it! Heavy stuff, boys—solid books."
"Yes, they worked all day and never played!" remarked the tall, round-faced peasant gravely, pointing with a knowing wink at the dictionaries stacked on top.

Not wanting to impose himself on the princess, Rostov didn't return to the house but stayed in the village to wait for her departure. When her carriage drove out, he mounted up and accompanied her eight miles from Bogucharovo to where the road was held by their own troops. At the inn at Yankovo he respectfully took his leave, for the first time allowing himself to kiss her hand.

"How can you say such things!" he said, blushing, in reply to Princess Mary's expressions of gratitude for her rescue, as she called what had happened. "Any policeman would have done the same! If we only had peasants to fight, we wouldn't have let the enemy get this far," he said with a sense of embarrassment and a desire to change the subject. "I'm only glad to have had the chance to meet you. Goodbye, Princess. I wish you happiness and consolation, and hope to see you again in happier circumstances. If you don't want to make me blush, please don't thank me!"

But the princess, even if she didn't thank him again in words, thanked him with her whole expression—her face radiant with gratitude and tenderness. She couldn't believe there was nothing to thank him for. On the contrary, she felt certain that if he hadn't been there, she would have been lost to the mutineers and the French, and that he had exposed himself to terrible and obvious danger to save her. Even more certain was she that he was a man of noble and lofty soul, able to understand her situation and her grief. His kind, honest eyes, with tears rising in them when she herself began to cry as she spoke of her loss, never left her memory.
When she had said goodbye and was alone, she suddenly felt her eyes filling with tears, and then, for the first time, a strange question presented itself: did she love him?

On the rest of the journey to Moscow, though her situation was not a cheerful one, Dunyasha, who rode with her in the carriage, more than once noticed that her mistress leaned out the window and smiled with an expression of mingled joy and sorrow.
"Well, suppose I do love him?" thought Princess Mary.

Ashamed as she was of admitting to herself that she had fallen in love with a man who might never love her back, she comforted herself with the thought that no one would ever know, and that she would not be to blame if, without ever speaking of it to anyone, she continued to the end of her life to love the man with whom she had fallen in love for the first and last time.

Sometimes when she recalled his looks, his sympathy, and his words, happiness did not seem impossible. It was at those moments that Dunyasha noticed her mistress smiling as she looked out the carriage window.
"Was it not fate that brought him to Bogucharovo, at that very moment?" thought Princess Mary. "And that made his sister refuse my brother?" In all this Princess Mary saw the hand of Providence.

The impression the princess made on Rostov was a very pleasant one. To remember her gave him pleasure, and when his comrades, hearing of his adventure at Bogucharovo, teased him about going to look for hay and instead picking up one of the wealthiest heiresses in Russia, he grew angry. He was angry precisely because the idea of marrying the gentle Princess Mary—who attracted him and had an enormous fortune—had more than once entered his mind against his will. For himself personally, Nicholas could not have wished for a better wife: marrying her would make his mother happy, would set his father's affairs in order, and would even—he felt it—ensure Princess Mary's happiness.
But Sonya? And his promise? That was why Rostov got angry when they teased him about Princess Bolkonskaya.
